title: Lesson 5: Overview of the Bible
description: The longest song in the Bible is a love song about God's Word. This lesson gives you the Bible's framework: a library of 66 books where every shelf points to Jesus.

blocks.text: In the last lesson, you saw that you are rooted in Jesus, and one of the deepest roots is the Word of God. The next three lessons belong together. This lesson gives you the framework, the next walks you through the Bible's one big story, and the third hands you the skill to dig into any passage on your own.

blocks.title: The Longest Song
blocks.text:
Near the middle of your Bible is the longest chapter in the whole book. It is not a list of laws or a battle story. It is a song, Psalm 119, and it runs 176 verses.

The writer built it like an alphabet poem. It has twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every line in a stanza begins with that letter. Many Bibles still print the letters as small headings: Aleph, Beth, Gimel. It is as if the writer wanted to praise God's Word from A to Z.

And nearly every verse does. He calls it God's word, His law, His promises, and His commands, and he talks about it the way you talk about someone you love: "Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day" (Psalm 119:97). Two of his lines are among the best-loved verses in the Bible:

"Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path." (Psalm 119:105)

"How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Psalm 119:103)

Here is the surprising part. The writer did not have the whole Bible you hold. He never read the Gospels, and he never heard the name Jesus. He had only part of God's library, and still he sang.
Carry this one sentence through the lesson: God's Word is a lamp for your path, and every shelf points to Jesus.
5.1 - What tends to keep the Bible on the shelf for you?
A Library, Not a Single Book

The Bible is not a single book but a library of 66 books, written by about 40 authors across roughly 1,500 years: kings, shepherds, fishermen, a doctor, a tax collector, and prophets. Yet the whole library tells one story from beginning to end, as you will see in the next lesson. That is because one Author stands behind every page:
All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
When you open the Bible, you are not reading someone's best guesses about life but words the living God intended for you to have.

Can a book copied by hand for centuries still be trusted? The psalmist sang, "Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens" (Psalm 119:89), and God has kept His Word on earth too, through careful copying and many manuscripts that scholars can compare. The Dead Sea Scrolls, copied before the time of Jesus, include a nearly complete Isaiah and show how carefully the Old Testament was kept. Most differences between copies are small slips of spelling or word order. You are opening a Word God has carried faithfully through time.
Old Testament and New Testament

The library has two main parts. The word "testament" means covenant, a binding promise between God and His people. The 39 books of the Old Testament tell how God created the world, chose a people, gave them His law, and promised that a Savior would come. The 27 books of the New Testament tell of that Savior arriving in Jesus, the birth of the church, and the hope of all things being made new.
The Old Testament can feel distant, but it is not a different story with a different God. It is the first half of the same story, and Jesus Himself treated every word of it as the Word of God.
Every book of the Bible fits on one shelf, arranged by section, and each section tells part of the one story.
5.2 - Which shelf of the library would you most like to explore, and why?
Every Shelf Points to Jesus
The library has many shelves, but it has one main subject. Jesus said this to some very careful Bible readers:
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.

You can know a lot about the Bible and still miss the point. The Law shows why people need a Savior. The History books show God keeping His promises through kings who never fully kept theirs. The Poetry gives words to the heart's longing, the Prophets point to a coming King, and the Gospels show Him. Every shelf points to Jesus.

The writer of Psalm 119 knew that longing. After 175 verses of loving God's Word, his song ends with a confession: "I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments" (Psalm 119:176). Loving the Bible did not make him perfect, but it taught him to ask God to come and find him. Jesus is the answer to that prayer: "For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10). The Bible is not a test you must pass. It is the voice of the Shepherd who comes looking for you.
Sweeter Than Honey

Look again at the line about honey. The psalmist is not describing homework but food. Jesus said the same thing when He was hungry in the wilderness: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matthew 4:4). God's Word is meant to be tasted, not just studied.

You do not have to understand everything the first time you open the Bible. Reading it is like switching on a lamp in a dark room. At first you only make out the basic shapes, but the longer you stay, the more your eyes adjust to the light. God's Word is living and active (Hebrews 4:12), so every time you read it, talk about it, and sit under it, more comes into focus, and it keeps getting better.
5.3 - What would it look like for God's Word to be written on your heart, not just read?
A Word on Translations

Every English Bible is translated from the Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek its books were first written in, and every translation team makes the same choice: stay as close as possible to the original words, or carry the original thought into natural English. Most translations sit somewhere along that line. Word-for-word translations like the NASB and ESV help with careful study. Thought-for-thought translations like the NIV and NLT help with steady reading.

blocks.text: This course quotes the ESV unless a lesson notes another translation. The best translation is the one you will actually open.
This Week's Practice

This week, take a book off three different shelves: Genesis 1 from the Law, Psalm 119:97-112 from Poetry and Wisdom, and John 1:1-18 from the Gospels. Before you read, pray the psalmist's short prayer: "Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law" (Psalm 119:18). Notice that Genesis 1 and John 1 begin with the same words. As you read each one, ask: How does this point me to Jesus?
Lesson 5 Review

You now have the framework. The Bible is a library of 66 books arranged in sections: Law, History, Poetry and Wisdom, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, Letters, and Revelation. The Old Testament promises, and the New Testament shows God keeping every promise in Jesus. The writer of Psalm 119 sang over part of that library, and you get to hold all of it. God's Word is a lamp for your path, and every shelf points to Jesus.
In the next lesson, you will follow the one big story that ties the whole library together.
